overview: Sweden and Norway shared a king from 1814 until 1905, but they were not simply one country. Norway kept its constitution, parliament and much domestic self-government, while disputes over the monarch and foreign affairs sharpened over time. A child in this era might help on a farm, learn to read, hear folktales, fear smallpox, or trek to a cold outdoor privy. Those experiences differed by class, place and language; Sami children in Norway faced forced assimilation in school. Norway declared the union dissolved in 1905 and Sweden accepted independence after negotiations. The imported map interval, about 1815 to 1914, outlasts the real union.

periods.title: Two kingdoms, one crown
periods.summary: Norway entered a personal union with Sweden while keeping its constitution and elected parliament.

periods.title: School and social change
periods.summary: Schooling, migration and town growth changed families while national culture and political disagreement developed.

periods.title: Parliament and the union question
periods.summary: Norwegian parliamentarianism strengthened and the dispute over separate consuls brought the union to an end.

items.text: In 1814 Norway left its old union with Denmark, adopted a constitution and fought a short war with Sweden. The settlement joined Norway and Sweden under one king, but Norway kept its own parliament and much control over home affairs.

The Norwegian constitution said “Kongeriget Norge er et frit, selvstændigt, udeleligt og uafhændeligt Rige.” That means Norway was a free, independent, indivisible and inalienable realm. Its next words placed it in union with Sweden under one king.

Norway’s parliament gained leverage in a long struggle with the king. In 1884 the monarch had to appoint a Norwegian government backed by the parliamentary majority, a breakthrough for parliamentarianism.

Norwegian shipping and trade made separate consuls abroad a major issue. When King Oscar II refused a Norwegian consular law, Norway’s parliament declared the union dissolved on 7 June 1905. Sweden recognized independence after a referendum and negotiations.
Women could not vote in the 1905 referendum, yet Norwegian women organized 244,765 signatures for separation. It was impressive political action by people the ballot box had excluded.

On a Swedish farm in the 1890s, children might fetch wood and water, mind younger siblings, pick berries or help with animals. Parents and children all worked; family labor mattered even when school attendance was expected.

Sweden’s 1842 school ordinance expanded basic schooling. By late century a child was expected to spend years in school, but farm work could interrupt lessons. A desk and a milk pail could compete for the same afternoon.

An 1826 diary by Swedish parsonage daughter Sofi Rönnqvist mentions reading aloud, coffee visits, dances, illness and caring for her father. It is a rare peek at one family’s social life, not a portrait of every household.
In Norway, Asbjørnsen and Moe collected folktales as people argued over national identity. A story told by a fire could end up in a book and become part of a wider debate about what was “Norwegian.”

A Norwegian women’s reading association founded in 1874 shared books, lectures and reading circles. Access to education and universities was unequal; friends making a library together was a way to open a door.

The two kingdoms also included Sami homelands. Norwegian authorities increasingly pressed Sami pupils to use Norwegian in school, especially later in the century. A classroom could therefore threaten a child’s home language.

Late nineteenth-century Norwegian towns grew around factories and processing of fish and timber, while many Swedish people emigrated because of hardship and scarce land. The union era was no single rural picture.

sections.title: Health, washing and the toilet question

items.text: Sweden began smallpox vaccination in the early nineteenth century. That was a real tool against a dangerous infection, though families still faced other illnesses and unequal access to care.

Heating water to wash bodies and laundry took time and fuel. In Norway the 1860 health law and public baths were part of a hygiene campaign; private bathrooms remained mainly for wealthier homes late in the century.
In parts of rural Norway even an outhouse was uncommon in the mid-nineteenth century. Many people simply went outdoors. A grand royal palace tells you very little about a farm child’s bathroom break.

Stockholm households mostly used courtyard dry privies, and waste could contaminate wells. Water-flush toilets reached only a small number of wealthy homes by 1895. Keeping drinking water away from waste mattered more than fancy porcelain.

ending.text: The Swedish-Norwegian union ended in 1905. Norway became an independent kingdom after its parliament’s declaration, referendum and negotiations with Sweden. Both kingdoms and their peoples continued; the imported map label extends to 1914 even though the shared monarchy did not.
